title: Origin of photosynthesis
summary: Photosynthesis lets organisms turn sunlight into chemical energy. Tice and Lowe describe photosynthetic microbial mats living 3,416 million years ago in what is now South Africa. A later MIT study finds that oxygen-producing photosynthesis, which MIT News calls Earth's single most important evolutionary innovation, likely evolved between 3.4 and 2.9 billion years ago.

uncertainty.note: Buck Reef Chert microbial mats are dated to 3,416 Ma (Tice & Lowe 2004); MIT phylogenomic clock models date the emergence of oxygenic cyanobacteria to between 3.4 and 2.9 Ga.

as_recorded.calendar: U-Pb zircon geochronology on volcanic tuffs bounding the Buck Reef Chert
as_recorded.value: photosynthetic organisms had evolved and were living in a stratified ocean supersaturated in dissolved silica 3,416 Myr ago

as_recorded.calendar: horizontal gene transfer and molecular clock model
as_recorded.value: oxygenic photosynthesis likely evolved between 3.4 and 2.9 billion years ago

where.modern_name: No single place; stand-in pin at Barberton, South Africa
where.historical_name: Barberton greenstone belt ocean floor, Paleoarchean Earth; euphotic microbial mats

paleo.not_applicable: Predates plate reconstructions; global Paleoarchean metabolic evolution.

importance.justification: The invention of photosynthesis expanded global primary biomass production by orders of magnitude and laid the biochemical foundation for the Great Oxidation Event and aerobic respiration.

related.because: Primitive chemotrophic cellular life provided the metabolic precursors from which light-driven photophosphorylation evolved.
Sustained oxygen production by photosynthetic cyanobacteria eventually overwhelmed geochemical reducing sinks and oxygenated the atmosphere.

reviewer_note: Dates are estimates, and the earliest forms did not produce oxygen. The pin at Barberton marks the fossil mats, not where photosynthesis began.
